title: Silent Hill-Like Uses Phones To Parry, Because Even Anime Girls Know Tech Is A Weapon
description: The survival-horror genre was born about 30 years ago, when people were scared of long shadows in Resident Evil's mansion, or of Silent Hill's medical gauzy fog -- but we've since moved on to more insidious enemies. There are data breaches from Meta, AI-generated restaurant menus that make burritos look like they've been shot with a gun, and other evidence that technology is constantly distorting and desecrating our lives. Upcoming Silent Hill-ish horror game Signal Veil understands the weight of that, so its protagonist uses a little flip phone as her weapon. Aki, who could pass as another vapid anime schoolgirl if it weren't for the sleepy bruises under her eyes, looks terrified to be alone in a new trailer revealed during Insider Gaming's 28 Games Later Horror Showcase. But, even when she's being pursued by a fleshy monstrosity, she isn't really by herself -- she has her mom's dainty, vintage cell phone, which players can use to physically attack enemies in a unique combat system. Developer Time Hunters tells Insider Gaming in an interview, "We grew up loving classic horror games like Resident Evil, but for Signal Veil we wanted to lean much more into psychological horror." So, as the Silent Hill franchise's crackling radio did for many of its main characters, Aki's cell phone shivers and hisses whenever it detects a monster. The sound is enough to make you, the player, paranoid, but Signal Veil's sanity system takes fear further by giving Aki's fraying mind gameplay consequences. "As her mental state deteriorates, the way she fights becomes more desperate, aggressive, and messy," Signal Veil developers say. Her teeny cell phone can knock enemies' heads around, or even use its camera flash to stun enemies and leave them open to a parry. "We really like games with parry systems, so at some point we thought, 'What if you could use the phone to parry an enemy?'" devs say. "It was one of those ideas that sounded strange at first, but once we tried it, we loved it."…

How Silent Hill: Townfall’s “Creepy Game Boy” Weaponizes Nostalgia For The Better
description: . I have a complicated relationship with the 1990s, an era remembered for its hazy pre-HD tech and early signs of broader connectivity without the mentally taxing standard of an always-online world. Lately, I've found the aesthetics of that era calling to me in the books I read, the shows I watch, and even in my social media feeds that regularly spit out "remember when?" reels that dredge up imagery of classrooms and malls that I never actually set foot in yet feel familiar. Instagram seems to think I'm simply nostalgic for this stuff, not understanding that I actually find it very eerie, snapshots of a childhood I can hardly recall for complicated reasons. And yet, I'm mesmerized by it. Most recently, I felt that same pull in Screen Burn's Silent Hill: Townfall. Whereas games like Silent Hill and Silent Hill 2 were set roughly in their respective modern days and are today revered as dreary time capsules, Townfall resurrects similar vibes, in turn revealing which parts stick out most to the team performing that necromancy. In a recent conversation with the studio's co-founder and Townfall's writer, Jon McKellan, he told me how Screen Burn sought to weaponize a particular type of nostalgia through the game's handheld CRTV device, and why the 1990s remain the ideal backdrop for a horror story. GameSpot: When Silent Hill: Townfall was first revealed, I wondered if it would be primarily a "gizmo" kind of game, like Stories Untold. Observation has a lot of physical interaction like that, too. What is it the team likes about that sort of thing in games? Jon McKellan: I think with horror, having something recognisable and tangible just sort of grounds you in the world a little bit more. People might not ever have owned one, but we all can understand the sensation of holding a little screen in our hands that shows us scary things! I’ve always loved analogue video aesthetics, and it’s been a big part of my own art style through my career, so the idea of making an entire…

title: PSA: Please Allow My Very Expensive Steam Frame Mistake To Help You, Fellow Glasses Wearers
description: The reservation/queue process for Steam Frame continues, with those lucky enough to be randomly selected already able to receive their orders. I'm just such a person, and it turns out I can't use the damned thing. I wear glasses. I apparently wear the wrong glasses, because they refuse to fit inside the Steam Frame. I was aware that the Frame ships with an optional spacer meant for glasses wearers, providing a bit more space between your glasses and the displays themselves. I expected to use this, even if it resulted in additional light bleeding in around my nose, as I often find to happen with VR headsets. In addition to the headset, I opted for the ergonomic accessories kit, which includes an extended light blocker that I hoped would mitigate that issue. Maybe it ultimately will, but I won't be finding out for some time. My typical approach of presuming this kind of situation would just be fine, because surely it has to, has failed me here. In trying to place the Frame on my head, with or without the spacer, the front of the headset bangs into my too-wide glasses. While I was concerned with having enough space between my face and the screen, it is actually the sheer width that is the problem: one that prevents use of the headset, not just one that is a mild annoyance. Check out my new desk decorations This is, to be clear, my own fault: There is a maximum width for eyeglasses buried in the specs for the Frame (140mm), but my assumption that a lack of problems in the past meant I'd be fine here has burned me (mine appear to be about 146mm wide). I've used PlayStation VR and Meta Quest devices successfully with glasses, but Frame's interior is either smaller than those or, as I continue to buy new glasses, I'm on a faster track to looking like Jiminy Glick than I realized. There is a solution, as in addition to the accessories that Valve itself sells, the company has collaborated with Zenni to offer prescription lenses that can be installed to avoid any need for…

title: PS5’s Exciting New Zelda-Like Kena Game Just Got Delayed
description: Developer Ember Lab has announced that its upcoming PS5 game Kena: Scars of Kosmora, the sequel to 2021's much-loved Kena: Bridge of Spirits, has been delayed. The game-- which gives off major Zelda vibes --was previously set to release this year, but now it's been delayed to 2027. In a blog post, the developers said they need more time to "deliver a top-notch game that exceeds the quality" of Bridge of Spirits. "Pushing our release into 2027 gives us the ability to really polish the expanded game experience we want to deliver," the studio said. Scars of Kosmora is a linear adventure game, just like the 2021 entry, but the sequel has a "broader and deeper scope," the studio said. "We hope you’re just as excited to jump into Kena’s next adventure as we are to share it with you. We’ve been working hard to fill it with the wonder, charm, and challenge fans have come to expect," the team added. "We appreciate your patience and support as we take the time for Scars of Kosmora to be the evolution of Kena’s journey and experience we want to deliver." In Scars of Kosmora, main character Kena is now a seasoned spirit guide and embarks on a journey to the island of Kosmora to find a "cure for her affliction and to reconnect with a friend from her past." The island holds a "powerful corruption" that fractures her staff, so Kena adopts a new method of manipulating the elements to her advantage. "On her journey, Kena discovers and nurtures memorable spirit companions-- whose powers she will harness to solve puzzles and defeat enemies using new elemental abilities," reads a line from the game's description. 2021's Bridge of Spirits was released initially on PS4, PS5, and PC, and later came to Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S in 2024. A Switch 2 edition arrived in March this year. Kosmora has been confirmed only for PS5 and PC so far.

title: GTA 6’s Weather System Sounds Like A Big Step Up
description: Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 includes a number of updates and improvements over the developer's past games, and that includes new weather systems. Rockstar's vice president of art for lighting and rendering at Rockstar, Owen Shepherd, told Game Informer that the studio has "re-engineered" the studio's weather system to "make everything more more localized and persistent." He said the goal was to make the weather in GTA 6's setting of Leonida--a stand-in for Florida--feel "dynamically solid and achieve a sense of scale" that the studio has never done before. GTA 6 launches on November 19. What that means in practice is that GTA 6 will have "fully dynamic cloudscapes that roll across the map" to provide a "broad spectrum of weather" in the game. Florida is known for its heat and humidity, along with its localized and fast-moving rain systems. Look one direction and you may see bright sunshine. Look the other and you could see a downpour. GTA 6 will replicate this with localized rain showers, along with rainbows that appear. Additionally, places where it recently rained in the game will remain wet, with puddles also popping up. GTA 6 also has a new wind system that includes "offshore breezes after sunset, convectional updrafts, and occlusion from buildings,” Shepherd said. “Hair and debris will swirl around on rooftops; gusts of wind will blow ripples over the water surface and bend the grass in swamps.” GTA 6 will also include tropical storms and hurricanes, along with thunder and lightning. Shepherd did not, however, get into how GTA 6's new weather systems could affect gameplay. Florida is known to experience devastating hurricanes, but it remains to be seen if, for example, a hurricane could knock down structures or trees. GTA 6 launches on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, priced at $80 for its standard edition and $100 for the Ultimate Edition. Rockstar is also selling a $400 collector's edition that includes a bunch of physical goodies, but not the game.

title: Blizzard Isn’t Fixing Diablo 4 Season 15’s Biggest Bug
description: Diablo 4 Season 15's biggest bug, one revolving around Hellfire Torch and being able to equip more Unique charms than should be possible, won't be fixed this season, Blizzard has announced. Hellfire Torch is a new Unique charm that counts as an extra set charm and comes with some great beneficial stats, like +All Skills, +All Stats, and +All Resistances. Players can usually only have one Unique charm equipped at a time, but Hellfire Torch breaks that rule, allowing players to use it and another Unique charm. That's strong on its own, but there is currently a bugged interaction with Hellfire Torch that is allowing players to equip two Unique charms in addition to Hellfire Torch instead of one, granting even higher levels of power. The bug seems to stem from Hellfire Torch being used first alongside the Seal of the Golden Epiphany, which allows players to equip up to three Unique charms. However, players are later swapping out Golden Epiphany for the Mythic Seal of the Diamond Mind, a seal that reduces the number of charms needed for set bonuses, but are still able to benefit from having additional Unique charms equipped. That, in turn, allows players to gain advantages from a full five-piece set bonus, Hellfire Torch, and two Unique charms all at once. Now, Diablo 4 design director Dan Tanguay in a forum post said Blizzard is aware of the bug and said Hellfire Torch' s current behavior is "beyond what was originally intended." That being said, Blizzard will be letting it ride this season as it works towards a fix in the future. "We know many players have spent significant time earning the Hellfire Torch and building characters around it," Tanguay said. "Because of that, we want to be thoughtful about making adjustments mid-season that could disrupt those investments." Tanguay continued: "We've also seen the positive reception to the Hellfire Torch itself from many players. The item has created a lot of excitement this season, and we've taken note of the feedback…

title: PS5 Just Got A PS5 Pro-Like AI Upgrade, But Don’t Expect It Everywhere Yet
description: The base PS5 console is no slouch when it comes to games, but compared to the PS5 Pro, it doesn't pack the same visual punch. That could change soon, as Sony has unveiled a new AI-upscaling upgrade for the older machine called Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR). Like PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR), it is designed to make games look sharper and maximize performance. While PSSR will still remain the "gold standard" for what Sony games can look like on PS5 Pro, QSSR looks like it'll offer a noticeable improvement on PS5. A result of the AI graphics collaboration with AMD, Sony says that it offers a "streamlined neural network architecture" for games. The only catch? For now, only two PS5 games will support it: Marvel's Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei --which is getting a new Complete Edition this month. Here are a few samples of it in action: "QSSR adds more pixel-level clarity and stability to our environments, bringing out extra detail amidst the busy streets of Madripoor, the dense alleyways of Shinjuku, and many other areas across Logan's epic journey. It’s a perfect companion to the launch of Marvel's Wolverine, and it brings a great taste of the PS5 Pro experience to our players on PS5," head of technology at Insomniac Games, Mike Fitzgerald, wrote in a PS Blog post. Jasmin Patry, lead rendering engineer at Ghost of Yotei developer Sucker Punch Productions, added that QSSR excels at "resolving the fine details" in characters and environments that previously wasn't possible on the base PS5. Both PS5 exclusives are receiving a patch today to add QSSR as an additional graphics option, and Sony says it will be offered to all PlayStation developers soon. If it's implemented widely and across many more games, QSSR could become a big selling point for the PS5, as the console will be six years old in November. Price hikes have made it more expensive to jump into the current console generation, and for anyone who can afford the $900 PS5 Pro, stock seems…

title: Here’s Your Chance To Get Monster Hunter Stories 3 And Two Other Steam Games For Just $5
description: While the dodging, slicing, and carving of your standard Monster Hunter affair is great fun, the Monster Hunter Stories spin-off series gives you more to love about this… monster-hunting world. Instead of grinding for materials to create stronger builds, Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection puts a greater focus on narrative, with gameplay that resembles Pokemon rather than the familiar action-RPG style of the mainline entries. If you want to give this under-loved spin-off a shot, you have the chance to get it and two other Steam games for under $5 in Fanatical’s latest bundle. Instead of playing as a hunter in this spin-off of one of the best RPG series around, you play as a Rider, and instead of carving up the carcasses of those bountiful hunts, you’ll be bonding with and raising monsters to become, effectively, your pets. The narrative sees you caught between two warring countries, but then you find an egg containing a thought-to-be-extinct Rathalos, which seems promising. Until, well, it’s a pair of Rathalos (Rathalosi?) that are fated to bring about the end of the world. Fun times. As I mentioned before, the combat isn’t what Monster Hunter fans will expect. Battles are turn-based affairs that see monsters duke it out, while the focus is on treating the world with respect instead of dealing with monsters in more… violent ways. It’s a lovely change from the usual Monster Hunter routine, and for that reason, it feels distinct enough that, while I wait for the Monster Hunter Wilds DLC, I don’t feel like I’m playing just another game from the series. It’s no surprise that our Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection review is so positive, with Jake Dekker saying that the game “easily stands shoulder to shoulder with some of the best Monster Hunter games” and giving it a 9/10 score. Not enough fans of the franchise have given it a chance, and, well, now’s the opportunity to fix that mistake. Right now, you have a chance at getting Monster Hunter Stories…

title: The Xbox Cloud Gaming Controller Is Dead, Apparently
description: Microsoft agreed to several big changes to appease regulators in its effort to get the blockbuster $75.4 billion deal to buy Activision Blizzard approved, including tweaks to its cloud-gaming projects. Now, more than a year later, we're still learning more about this, including a new claim from The New York Times that Microsoft canceled plans for a new Xbox controller "devoted to cloud gaming." A spokesperson for Microsoft denied that the controller concept was abandoned due to the regulatory process, but did not provide a reason. Microsoft never formally announced or unveiled any controller for cloud gaming, but an image of it leaked this year, prompting raised eyebrows for its... unique design. Microsoft cut deals with a variety of companies--including Ubisoft, Nware, EE, Boosteroid, Ubitus, and Nvidia --to help mitigate concerns from the UK's Competition & Markets Authority (CMA) that Microsoft might give preferential treatment to its own cloud gaming networks. Former Xbox CEO Phil Spencer, who led Xbox during the sale process, said such deals freed up one of the concerns the CMA had and helped bring more games to more people. The Xbox cloud-gaming service showed some initial signs of growth, but the program suffered a setback recently when Microsoft announced that it will soon put limits on how much people can use the service, and then charge them more to keep playing. Additionally, Windows Central recently discovered that the dedicated cloud gaming app for older Samsung TVs will go away soon due to a compatibility issue. Access to cloud gaming is one of the perks of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, allowing people to stream their games. Later this year, people will be able to buy game time for cloud gaming on Xbox without a Game Pass membership. One of the appeals of cloud gaming, at least in theory, is that it requires no expensive local hardware like an Xbox or PC, both of which are more expensive than ever due to the AI-fueled demand for memory and components.…

title: RetroSpace offers a huge sci-fi playground for inquisitive space janitors, but I'm not that System Shocked by the tools at your disposal
description: In my time as a videogame partaker, I have crawled through approximately three billion airvents. I may well have crawled through more vents than you've had hot dinners. As such, any videogame that can get me excited about loosening a barred hatch and hauling my heavy ass into a square tunnel is doing something right. The Wild Gentlemen's new sci-fi immersive sim RetroSpace gives pretty fair vent. It hides them all over. You'll walk along a dilapidated, meandering corridor and your eye will be caught by a certain combination of shadows, flirtatiously screened by pipes. 'Can I fit behind there?' You ask yourself, and lo, you have revealed a shortcut to the head engineer's office. Elsewhere, switches peek from behind stacks of luggable crates, and bent guard-rails draw your eye to a footwide ledge leading around the next pillar. In general, RetroSpace does a nice job of squirrelling secrets into even the smallest chambers, and if the secret is very often a "rocket doughnut" or other inventory-clogging flotsam, sensing the prize and snuffling after it is a thrill. I hope the thrill will intensify as RetroSpace goes on, perhaps leaving a few of its obvious influences behind. Read more

title: I'm not sure the "AI" in my chair's lumbar support actually counts as AI, but it has been smart enough to help my posture
description: Note from James, 02/10: We've heard your complaints that some of the wording in this piece - a lot of which, if I'm honest, was added/changed by me in the edit - overstates the chair's potential health benefits. The HBADA’s X7 chair may reduce back pain during long periods of sitting at your desk but it will not literally fix your spine. While it is and will remain the RPS way to indulge in some occasional hyperbole, we don't want to suggest that swivel chairs cure physical conditions, so I've clarified these bits to avoid confusion. AI is everywhere, exhausting to keep up with, and increasingly perceived as harmful to games. But that’s mostly generative AI; the more limited, less media-scraping and energy-hungry breeds of artificial intelligence can still play a harmless, maybe even useful role, especially on the hardware side. Even if it finds itself in some unexpected places, as is the case with HBADA’s X7 chair. While AI-powered lumbar support sounds like the kind of gimmicky nonsense that’s become all too common in 2026, I’ve been using an X7 for a week, and it’s... surprisingly effective? Definitely for straightening up my posture, which I'm hopeful will help with my recurring back pain issues. It’s been a very pleasant surprise. Read more
